html:
Isabella Bird, an English travel writer, spent three days and two nights in the house of an Ainu chief at Biratori in Hokkaido in August 1878. She was 46 and had one companion, her Japanese interpreter Ito. Japan had begun to settle the island after the Meiji Restoration. Her letters home became the book Unbeaten Tracks in Japan. She writes "Aino" for Ainu.

I told them that I came from a land in the sea, very far away, where they saw the sun go down—so very far away that a horse would have to gallop day and night for five weeks to reach it—and that I had come a long journey to see them, and that I wanted to ask them many questions, so that when I went home I might tell my own people something about them. … Before they told me anything they begged and prayed that I would not inform the Japanese Government that they had told me of their customs, or harm might come to them!
About nine the stew was ready, and the women ladled it into lacquer bowls with wooden spoons. The men were served first, but all ate together. … My candles had been forgotten, and our séance was held by the fitful light of the big logs on the fire, aided by a succession of chips of birch bark, with which a woman replenished a cleft stick that was stuck into the fire-hole.
